title: AI Data Centers Consume Power US Factories Desperately Need
summary: AI data centers are converting old aluminum smelters, consuming massive power while US manufacturers struggle. A $9 trillion infrastructure boom threatens
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- AI data centers are converting abandoned US aluminum smelters, consuming up to 635 megawatts per facility while manufacturers struggle with high electricity costs.
- Columbia economist estimates $9 trillion AI infrastructure investment through 2032, exceeding 19th century railroad expansion as percentage of economy.
- Data centers pay $115 per megawatt-hour for power while aluminum smelters need $40 rates to compete globally, creating impossible economics for US manufacturing revival.


Abandoned aluminum smelters across the United States are becoming battlegrounds in an energy war between artificial intelligence infrastructure and manufacturing revival. As AI companies convert idle industrial facilities into massive data centers, they are consuming electricity that domestic factories desperately need to compete globally, creating an impossible economic conflict for policymakers.


Officially launched on November 24, 2026, this documented trend reveals how AI's appetite for power is fundamentally reshaping American industrial strategy and threatening manufacturing jobs the current administration promised to restore.


## The $9 Trillion Infrastructure Transformation


Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimates the cost of building data centers, power supplies, and computing equipment through 2032 at nearly $9 trillion. As a share of the economy, this investment surge would exceed even the 19th century expansion of the railroads, representing the largest infrastructure build-out in modern American history.


Developers are scouring the country for sites with transmission lines, substations, and grid connections that can get new facilities online quickly. Old aluminum smelters, built around access to huge amounts of electricity, have become prime targets. The economics are stark: data centers can sustain operations at power prices near $115 per megawatt-hour, while a new US aluminum smelter would need decades of electricity priced near $40 to be globally competitive.


## Massena: Ground Zero for the Power Conflict


In Massena, New York, the closed Alcoa East smelter illustrates the transformation. New York Digital Investment Group (NYDIG) wants to convert the sprawling complex into a data center consuming as much as 635 megawatts of electricity, enough to supply more than half a million American homes. The facility, which began as a Bitcoin mining operation in 2018, represents precisely what makes abandoned smelters attractive to AI companies.


Mayor Gregory Paquin faces an impossible choice. The town's population has fallen to 12,400 residents, businesses have disappeared, and the municipal budget faces cuts to fire, sanitation, and essential services. NYDIG promises 200 permanent jobs, 2,000 construction positions, $75 million in grid upgrades, and status as the village's largest taxpayer. Yet opponents have packed town meetings, displaying signs reading "You can't drink data" and questioning whether promised economic benefits justify the costs.


## Manufacturing Economics Collapse Under AI Demand


The aluminum industry reveals the brutal mathematics. Century Aluminum sold its idled Hawesville, Kentucky smelter earlier in 2026 for $200 million in cash to TeraWulf, which is converting it into a data center with Anthropic signed on under a 20-year power lease. "One of the biggest challenges in developing[AI data centers](https://emergent.sh/news/400-us-ai-data-centers-use-more-power-than) today is securing power within a commercially viable time frame," says Kerri Langlais, TeraWulf's chief strategy officer. "Sites with established electrical infrastructure and a realistic path to near-term power availability are increasingly rare."


For aluminum producers, the power price gap is insurmountable. US manufacturers now pay the highest aluminum prices in the world following 50% tariffs on Canadian imports. Alcoa has earned $3.5 billion in aluminum profits over six quarters by selling Quebec-made metal to the US at inflated prices. Meanwhile, domestic beer maker Deschutes Brewery reports tariffs have extracted $3 million from its business, with CEO Peter Skrbek noting there is "no good way to protect yourself" from the Midwest premium price increases.


## Secondary Production: A Potential Alternative


Some industry leaders advocate for secondary aluminum production as a solution. These facilities recycle existing aluminum in natural-gas-fired furnaces rather than consuming massive electricity for primary smelting. Matt Rohm, CEO of MX Holdings, points to the steel industry's transformation through electric arc furnaces as a model.


Secondary producers already account for 80% of US aluminum production and can be operational within 18 to 24 months. Nucor, which started with a single mini mill in 1969, is now America's biggest steel producer, with mini mills accounting for over 70% of raw steel production. "We should be thinking more of the mini mill concept and geographically putting supply closer to where demand is," Rohm says.


However, Rohm warns that high aluminum prices driven by tariffs are destroying demand, pushing manufacturers toward alternatives like steel for products ranging from soda cans to flatbed trailers.


## Policy Collision and Future Implications


President Donald Trump's administration faces competing priorities: pushing rapid data center build-out while trying to revive US aluminum production for national security. Since returning to office, Trump has imposed tariffs on foreign aluminum and backed a $4 billion Oklahoma smelter that would be the first in the US since 1980. "This country desperately needs aluminum," Trump said in August. "We don't have it."


The Democrats' massive victories in the 2026 US midterm elections highlighted this tension. Voters rebelled against both tariffs because of their impact on consumer prices and energy-hogging data centers. New York Governor Kathy Hochul imposed a statewide moratorium on certain large data center developments, though local officials believe Massena may be exempt because NYDIG had received permits before the moratorium.


## What This Means


The conversion of abandoned smelters into AI infrastructure represents an irreversible shift in American industrial priorities. With data centers willing to pay nearly triple what manufacturers can afford for electricity, the economics of domestic metals production have collapsed. Towns like Massena face stark choices between accepting AI facilities that provide tax revenue but limited jobs, or maintaining industrial nostalgia while municipal budgets crumble. As Mayor Paquin puts it bluntly: "Either you adapt or you die." The $9 trillion AI infrastructure boom is not just reshaping the energy grid but fundamentally rewriting which industries can survive on American soil, with manufacturing increasingly priced out of its own power supply.
